msc-21069+3845.name: 61 Cygni
msc-21069+3845.introduction: is a pair of orange dwarf stars about 11.4 light-years away in Cygnus. Both are cooler and fainter than the Sun, and their mutual orbit takes centuries.

sections.title: The first reliable stellar distance
sections.text: In 1838, Friedrich Bessel used the tiny annual shift of 61 Cygni against background stars to measure its distance. This was the first published reliable parallax distance to a star beyond the Sun, turning the scale of interstellar space into something measurable.

sections.title: Piazzi’s Flying Star
sections.text: Its conspicuous motion across the sky earned it the nickname “Flying Star.” The two members also serve as reference stars for classifying K-dwarf spectra; despite their quiet appearance, they have magnetic activity cycles and can flare.

procyon.name: Procyon
procyon.introduction: is a bright binary in Canis Minor, about 11.4 light-years away. The light we see comes mainly from Procyon A, a yellow-white star beginning to evolve away from the main sequence; B is a faint white dwarf.

sections.title: A companion predicted before it was seen
sections.text: Irregularities in Procyon’s motion led Friedrich Bessel to infer an unseen companion in 1844. The difficult visual discovery of Procyon B followed in 1896. Today the pair’s roughly 41-year orbit helps astronomers measure the masses of both stars.

sections.title: Before the dog
sections.text: The name comes from Greek for “before the dog,” referring to its rising before Sirius, the Dog Star, from northern latitudes. Procyon, Sirius and Betelgeuse mark the Winter Triangle.

gj-725.name: Struve 2398
gj-725.introduction: is a binary of two red dwarfs in Draco, also known as GJ 725. The catalog’s HD 173739 and HD 173740 are its A and B components.

sections.title: A slow dance nearby
sections.text: The stars are only about 11.5 light-years away, but both require optical aid to see. Their wide orbit takes many centuries, allowing long-term observations of two low-mass stars formed together.

sections.title: Faint in visible light, active in X-rays
sections.text: Both components emit X-rays from hot outer atmospheres. Their rapid apparent motion across the sky is another reminder that an inconspicuous point of light can be one of our closest neighbors.

gj-15.name: Groombridge 34
gj-15.introduction: is a wide pair of red dwarfs about 11.6 light-years away in Andromeda. It is also called GJ 15; GX Andromedae is A and GQ Andromedae is B.

sections.title: Two variable stars
sections.text: Both members can brighten in magnetic flares. Although they travel together through space, they are separated by roughly a hundred Earth–Sun distances and take about a millennium to orbit their common center of mass.

sections.title: Planets around A
sections.text: Radial-velocity observations support a small planet on an approximately 11.4-day orbit and a much more distant companion with a period of roughly 20 years. The inner signal was disputed before longer observations recovered it, illustrating the difficulty of separating planets from stellar activity.

10pc-0039.name: DX Cancri
10pc-0039.introduction: is a very small red dwarf in Cancer, also called GJ 1111. Although only about 11.7 light-years away, it is much too faint to see without a telescope.

sections.title: A fast-spinning flare star
sections.text: DX Cancri rotates in roughly half a day. Its magnetic eruptions can briefly increase its brightness severalfold. The variable-star name DX Cancri was assigned after its changing brightness was recognized in the 1980s.

sections.title: Near the bottom of the main sequence
sections.text: It has only about a tenth of the Sun’s mass. Its cool, molecule-rich atmosphere and tiny energy output make it very different from a scaled-down yellow star.

msc-22034-5647.name: Epsilon Indi
msc-22034-5647.introduction: is a nearby family containing an orange dwarf, Epsilon Indi A, and the much fainter brown dwarfs Ba and Bb. It lies about 12 light-years away in Indus.

sections.title: Two brown dwarfs for comparison
sections.text: Ba and Bb orbit one another far from A. Their different T-type spectra let astronomers compare cooler and warmer methane-rich atmospheres in objects sharing the same wider stellar environment.

sections.title: A cold giant seen by Webb
sections.text: A also hosts the giant planet Epsilon Indi Ab. Webb observations released in 2024 detected the planet’s own mid-infrared light, making it a rare example of a cool, mature giant studied by direct imaging.

source.title: NASA: Webb images cold exoplanet 12 light-years away

10pc-0044.name: Tau Ceti
10pc-0044.introduction: is a nearby, solitary G-type star in Cetus, visible to the unaided eye. It resembles the Sun but is cooler, less luminous and poorer in heavy elements.

sections.title: An early SETI target
sections.text: Tau Ceti was one of the two stars observed in Frank Drake’s Project Ozma in 1960, an early radio search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Its proximity and broadly Sun-like character have kept it prominent in both astronomy and science fiction.

sections.title: Dust is certain; planets are harder
sections.text: A cold debris disk reveals material left over from collisions among smaller bodies. Several low-amplitude signals have been interpreted as planets, but their number and reliability remain disputed; the proposed worlds should not be treated as an established Earth-like planetary system.

10pc-0045.name: GJ 1061
10pc-0045.introduction: is a small red dwarf about 12 light-years away in Horologium. Its true proximity was established in 1997, after earlier estimates had placed it much farther away.

sections.title: Three small worlds
sections.text: The Red Dots project announced three close-orbiting planets in 2019. The outer planet, d, lies in the star’s conservative habitable zone, where suitable atmospheric conditions could allow liquid water; its actual climate is unknown.

sections.title: An old, slow spinner
sections.text: The star rotates slowly and shows relatively low activity. This makes it useful for precise searches for the tiny stellar wobbles caused by low-mass planets.

10pc-0049.name: YZ Ceti
10pc-0049.introduction: is a faint, active red dwarf in Cetus with three small planets on very short orbits. It is a separate star from the nearby Sun-like Tau Ceti.

sections.title: Years measured in days
sections.text: The planets complete their orbits in roughly two to five Earth days. Their compact arrangement makes them interesting examples of how several small worlds can fit close to a cool star.

sections.title: A possible magnetic connection
sections.text: Radio bursts reported in 2023 may arise from an interaction between the innermost planet and the star’s magnetic environment. A planetary magnetic field is one possible interpretation, rather than an established measurement of the planet’s surface conditions.

10pc-0053.name: Luyten’s Star
10pc-0053.introduction: is a nearby red dwarf in Canis Minor, also known as GJ 273. It lies only about 1.2 light-years from the much brighter Procyon system.

sections.title: A bright neighbor in its sky
sections.text: From Luyten’s Star, Procyon would shine about as brightly as Venus at its best in our sky. The reverse view would be much less impressive because Luyten’s Star gives off far less light.

sections.title: A nearby temperate-orbit target
sections.text: Its two established inner planets have years of about 4.7 and 18.6 days. The outer of these, GJ 273 b, receives roughly Earth-like irradiation, but its atmosphere, surface and habitability are unknown. Additional longer-period candidates remain unconfirmed.

10pc-0056.name: Teegarden’s Star
10pc-0056.introduction: is a tiny red dwarf in Aries, about 12.5 light-years away. It remained unrecognized as a close neighbor until 2003 despite moving conspicuously against the background sky.

sections.title: Found in an asteroid archive
sections.text: The discovery came from mining images taken by the Near-Earth Asteroid Tracking program. It is named after team leader Bonnard Teegarden, showing how data collected for one purpose can reveal something quite different.

sections.title: Small planets around a small star
sections.text: At least three planets are known, detected through the star’s radial-velocity wobble. Two were announced in 2019 and a third in 2024. Some orbit in or near the habitable zone, which describes irradiation rather than evidence for life.

10pc-0059.name: Kapteyn’s Star
10pc-0059.introduction: is a fast-moving, metal-poor red subdwarf in Pictor. Unlike most nearby stars, it belongs to the Milky Way’s old halo population.

sections.title: A visitor from an older Galaxy
sections.text: Its Galactic orbit runs opposite to the usual rotation of the disk. A proposed connection to the debris of the galaxy that supplied Omega Centauri is intriguing but remains an interpretation of its motion and composition.

sections.title: Planets that did not hold up
sections.text: Two planets were announced in 2014, including a supposed temperate super-Earth. Later work linked the signals to stellar activity, and a 2021 analysis rejected both planet interpretations.

10pc-0060.name: Lacaille 8760
10pc-0060.introduction: is the brightest M-type dwarf in Earth’s night sky, though still generally too faint for unaided viewing. It lies about 13 light-years away in Microscopium.

sections.title: An eighteenth-century entry
sections.text: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille observed it from the Cape of Good Hope. Its familiar number comes from a later edition of his catalog, illustrating how historical survey names survive alongside modern identifiers.

sections.title: Also called AX Microscopii
sections.text: The variable-star name refers to its flare activity. It is at the warmer, more luminous end of the red-dwarf population, rather than one of the tiny ultracool dwarfs that dominate the faintest nearby-star lists.

kruger-60.name: Krüger 60
kruger-60.introduction: is a pair of red dwarfs in Cepheus, about 13 light-years away. Their mutual orbit takes roughly 45 years.

sections.title: DO Cephei is the smaller companion
sections.text: The catalog’s DO Cephei is component B of this system. Its magnetic flares can last up to about an hour, so an observation made during an eruption can give a very different impression of its brightness.

sections.title: An orbit that weighs the stars
sections.text: Because the pair is close enough to follow through its orbit, astronomers can determine stellar masses from motion. Systems like this help anchor models of stars much less massive than the Sun.

scr-j1845-6357.name: SCR J1845−6357
scr-j1845-6357.introduction: pairs a very low-mass red dwarf with a cooler T-type brown dwarf in Pavo. At about 13 light-years, it offers a close comparison across the stellar–substellar boundary.

sections.title: A late addition to the neighborhood
sections.text: The primary was identified in the SuperCOSMOS survey in 2004. Its brown dwarf companion was reported in 2006, after high-resolution infrared observations separated the faint object from the star.

sections.title: Methane reveals the companion
sections.text: The brown dwarf absorbs strongly in methane bands, unlike the warmer primary. Imaging at selected infrared wavelengths helps distinguish its atmosphere from the overwhelming light of its stellar companion.

10pc-0065.name: DENIS J1048−3956
10pc-0065.introduction: is an ultracool dwarf in Antlia, close to the boundary between the smallest stars and brown dwarfs. The catalog lists its longer designation, DENIS J104814.6−395606.

sections.title: Nearby but overlooked
sections.text: It was recognized in the DENIS infrared survey in 2000, despite lying only about 13 light-years away. Its extremely weak visible light explains how such a close object could remain unnoticed.

sections.title: A powerful radio flare
sections.text: Radio observations reported in 2005 caught a dramatic flare. The event showed that even an object with such a cool atmosphere can maintain an energetic magnetic environment.

source.title: Burgasser & Putman 2005: Radio emission and a spectacular flare from DENIS 1048−3956

ross-614.name: Ross 614
ross-614.introduction: is a close red-dwarf binary in Monoceros, also called V577 Monocerotis. Both catalog components belong to the same system.

sections.title: A companion found through a wobble
sections.text: Frank Ross identified the moving star in the 1920s. A much fainter companion was inferred from astrometric motion in the 1930s, before it could be directly seen. The pair became an important early example of a low-mass astrometric binary.

sections.title: A difficult double
sections.text: The secondary is easily lost in the primary’s glare. Following their roughly 16-year orbit provides a way to test the relationship between the masses and luminosities of faint red dwarfs.

10pc-0068.name: UGPS J0722−0540
10pc-0068.introduction: is a cold T-type brown dwarf in Monoceros, discovered through UKIDSS in 2010, about 13 light-years away.

sections.title: Conditional physical estimates
sections.text: Its bolometric luminosity is about 0.00000063 times the Sun’s. At assumed ages of 1 and 5 billion years, evolutionary models give 502/539 K, 10.7/25.8 Jupiter masses and 1.0192/0.886 Jupiter radii, respectively. The displayed ranges connect these scenarios; age is unmeasured.

source.title: Dupuy & Kraus 2013, Science 341, 1492, Table S5

sections.title: Sources: adopted radial velocity
sections.text: Hood et al. (2023) obtain 35.80 −0.15/+0.16 km/s from FIRE spectroscopy. Star View adopts this velocity with a conservative ±0.16 km/s uncertainty. Their unphysically small fitted radius and dependent mass and temperature are withheld.

source.title: Hood et al. (2023): preferred FIRE retrieval and section 4.2

sections.title: Sources: earlier velocity analysis
sections.text: Bochanski et al. (2011) reported 46.9 ± 2.5 km/s from the same spectrum. This alternative is retained, not adopted; the disagreement does not establish changing velocity.

source.title: Bochanski et al. (2011): FIRE spectroscopy

sections.title: Infrared photometry
sections.text: JWST measured F480M = 12.016 ± 0.011 Vega mag on April 17, 2023; visual V remains unavailable.

source.title: Albert et al. (2025), Table 2
Dupuy & Kraus (2013): luminosity and evolutionary scenarios

10pc-0069.name: Wolf 1061
10pc-0069.introduction: is a red dwarf in Ophiuchus with three known planets. It is only about 14 light-years away but requires a telescope to see.

sections.title: A compact planetary system
sections.text: The planets were found in archival HARPS radial-velocity observations. Later analysis revised the outer planet’s orbit substantially, showing why long observing baselines matter even after a discovery is announced.

sections.title: Near a habitable-zone boundary
sections.text: Wolf 1061 c lies near the inner edge of the star’s habitable zone. That makes it interesting for climate studies, but does not establish that it has a rocky surface, liquid water or an Earth-like atmosphere.

10pc-0073.name: van Maanen’s Star
10pc-0073.introduction: is the nearest solitary white dwarf, about 14 light-years away in Pisces. Adriaan van Maanen discovered it in 1917.

source.title: Carnegie Science: A 1917 spectrum records evidence of an exoplanetary system

sections.title: A century-old clue to planetary debris
sections.text: A Mount Wilson spectrum from 1917 recorded calcium and other heavy elements in its atmosphere. These should sink below the surface, so their presence points to replenishment by rocky debris: evidence of extrasolar planetary material recorded decades before exoplanets were recognized. It did not identify an individual planet.

sections.title: Before it became a white dwarf
sections.text: A 2008 evolutionary study estimated a progenitor about 2.6 times the Sun’s mass, with a main-sequence lifetime of roughly 900 million years. Its giant phase may have expanded to a radius of roughly 4.6 AU. The model gives about 3.2 billion years of subsequent cooling and a total age near 4.1 billion years. These are model estimates, not direct measurements.

source.title: Burleigh et al. (2008): the DODO survey of van Maanen’s star

wolf-424.name: Wolf 424
wolf-424.introduction: is a pair of very low-mass red dwarfs in Virgo, also called FL Virginis. Both members are invisible to the unaided eye despite their proximity.

sections.title: A photographic double
sections.text: Dirk Reuyl recognized its binary nature in 1941 from the elongated appearance of the star on photographs. The two stars orbit in roughly 15–16 years, with a separation of only a few astronomical units.

sections.title: Two magnetic little stars
sections.text: Both components can flare. Their similar low masses and shared origin make them useful for comparing magnetic activity and stellar structure near the faint end of the main sequence.

10pc-0076.name: Gliese 1
10pc-0076.introduction: is the red dwarf listed here as HD 225213, in Sculptor. It is nearby but too faint to see without optical aid.

sections.title: Why it is number one
sections.text: Its position close to the zero point of right ascension at the catalog’s reference epoch placed it first in the Gliese nearby-star catalog and the Luyten Half-Second catalog. The number describes catalog ordering, not proximity.

sections.title: A fast traveler
sections.text: Its high proper motion was documented by Benjamin Gould in 1885. Its substantial motion relative to the Sun and eccentric path through the Galaxy distinguish it from stars moving on more nearly circular disk orbits.

10pc-0077.name: TZ Arietis
10pc-0077.introduction: is the red dwarf cataloged here as GJ 9066, also known as GJ 83.1. It is a small, magnetically active star in Aries.

sections.title: A giant around a tiny star
sections.text: Radial-velocity observations support a giant planet on an approximately 771-day, eccentric orbit. Finding such a substantial companion around a star with only a small fraction of the Sun’s mass challenges simple expectations about planet formation.

source.title: NASA Exoplanet Archive: GJ 9066, confirmed and refuted signals

sections.title: Names and false signals
sections.text: The confirmed outer planet is called GJ 9066 c in the NASA archive, while some papers call it TZ Ari b. Earlier short-period candidates were not upheld: one tracked stellar rotation, and the roughly 240-day signal was refuted.

10pc-0080.name: GJ 687
10pc-0080.introduction: is a nearby red dwarf in Draco, about 15 light-years away. Its slow rotation and modest activity have made it a target for precision planet searches.

sections.title: A Neptune-mass neighbor
sections.text: A planet announced in 2014 produces a stellar wobble with a period of about 38 days. Its minimum mass is comparable to Neptune’s, rather than Earth’s.

sections.title: A wider possible companion
sections.text: A second, longer-period planet signal was reported in 2020. It places a possible companion in a colder, more distant orbit; the short-period planet remains the better-established part of the system’s discovery history.

10pc-0082.name: GJ 674
10pc-0082.introduction: is a red dwarf in Ara with a close-orbiting planet discovered using HARPS in 2007. The planet completes a year in about 4.7 days.

sections.title: Spots can imitate planets
sections.text: The discovery analysis separated the planet’s short-period wobble from a longer signal associated with the star’s rotation. Photometry and activity indicators helped distinguish those two causes of changing radial velocity.

sections.title: Quiet does not mean flare-free
sections.text: Although less active than some famous flare stars, GJ 674 produced a strong ultraviolet flare observed in 2018. Such events matter when assessing the radiation environment of its close-in planet.

10pc-0084.name: WISE 1639−6847
10pc-0084.introduction: is a cold Y-type brown dwarf in Triangulum Australe, identified in WISE survey data in 2012. Its full designation is WISE J163940.83−684738.6.

sections.title: What “peculiar” means here
sections.text: Its Y0 pec classification flags unusual infrared colors and spectral peaks. Temperature estimates depend on the atmosphere and evolutionary models used.

sections.title: A test for atmosphere models
sections.text: Models struggle to reproduce its entire spectrum consistently. Peculiarity describes these spectral differences, not a visible feature on a resolved surface.

sections.title: Model estimates from infrared light
sections.text: Fontanive et al. (2023) infer 361 ± 14 K, 13 ± 4 Jupiter masses and log₁₀(L/L☉) = −6.82 ± 0.05. Their ATMO 2020 estimates assume a population age distribution of 5 ± 3 billion years; that is not a measured age. Radius is derived from the same temperature and luminosity.

source.title: Fontanive et al. (2023): HST photometry and evolutionary estimates

sections.title: Infrared measurements
sections.text: Hubble measured F127M = 20.00 ± 0.02 Vega mag in 2019. JWST measured F480M = 13.487 ± 0.005 in 2023. Infrared magnitudes cannot supply visual V.

source.title: Albert et al. (2025), Tables 2 and 4; Fontanive et al. (2023), Tables 2–3
Fontanive et al. (2023): HST photometry and evolutionary estimates

10pc-0085.name: LP 731−58
10pc-0085.introduction: is a very faint red dwarf in Sextans, also known as LHS 292 and GJ 3622. It lies about 15 light-years away.

sections.title: An inconspicuous flare star
sections.text: Its late M-type spectrum places it among the coolest nearby red dwarfs. It can suddenly brighten in magnetic flares even though its normal visible light is extremely weak. The alternative catalog names all refer to this same star.

10pc-0086.name: LAWD 37
10pc-0086.introduction: is an isolated white dwarf in Musca, also called LP 145−141, about 15 light-years away. It became the first solitary white dwarf whose mass was measured directly through gravitational microlensing.

sections.title: Weighed by bending starlight
sections.text: In 2019 it passed close to a distant star on the sky. Hubble measured the shift in that star’s apparent position as LAWD 37’s gravity bent its light. The 2023 analysis found a mass of 0.56 ± 0.08 times the Sun’s, without a binary companion.

source.title: NASA: Hubble directly measures the mass of a lone white dwarf

sections.title: A test of dense matter
sections.text: Combining that gravitational mass with the white dwarf’s radius tests the predicted mass–radius relation. In a white dwarf, adding mass generally makes the remnant smaller: its internal support comes from electron degeneracy.

source.title: McGill et al. (2023): testing the white dwarf mass–radius relation
McGill et al. (2023): weighing LAWD 37 through astrometric microlensing

gj-1245.name: GJ 1245
gj-1245.introduction: is a triple system of very low-mass red dwarfs in Cygnus, also called V1581 Cygni. A and C form the inner pair, with B farther out.

sections.title: A family with two scales
sections.text: The faint C component orbits close to A, while B follows a much wider orbit around the inner pair. The lettering can be misleading: the tight pair is A–C, rather than A–B.

sections.title: Flares from sibling stars
sections.text: A and B are active flare stars. Comparing members formed together helps astronomers explore how rotation and magnetic activity behave in stars close to the minimum mass needed for sustained hydrogen fusion.

10pc-0090.name: WISE 1741+2553
10pc-0090.introduction: is a very cool T9 brown dwarf in Hercules. The WISEP J174124.25+255319.5 catalog entry and the slightly different WISEPA designation refer to the same object.

sections.title: Found in WISE’s first discoveries
sections.text: Several teams identified and studied it in 2011 using WISE data and infrared follow-up observations. Its very weak visible light had hidden a neighbor only about 15 light-years away.

sections.title: Searching for hidden multiplicity
sections.text: Keck adaptive-optics observations searched for a close companion without resolving one. That result limits companions at the separations and brightnesses the observations could detect; it does not rule out every possible companion.

10pc-0091.name: Gliese 876
10pc-0091.introduction: is the red dwarf listed here as IL Aquarii. Its four-planet system is a classic example of strong gravitational interactions between exoplanets.

sections.title: A giant-planet milestone
sections.text: The discovery of Gliese 876 b in 1998 showed that a red dwarf could host a giant planet. Additional planets revealed a compact system with both giant and much smaller worlds.

sections.title: A celestial rhythm
sections.text: The three outer planets participate in a Laplace resonance: their orbital periods are close to a 1:2:4 pattern, related to the rhythm of Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa and Ganymede. Their mutual tugs are strong enough to help measure the system’s architecture.

10pc-0096.name: L 143−23
10pc-0096.introduction: is a faint red dwarf in Carina, also called LHS 288 and GJ 3618. Its small mass and cool surface keep it invisible to the unaided eye despite its proximity.

sections.title: An ambiguous astrometric hint
sections.text: A 2007 study suggested a possible massive planet from changes in the star’s apparent position. A chance overlap with an unrelated faint background star could mimic the effect, so the claim was not a secure planet detection.

10pc-0097.name: GJ 1002
10pc-0097.introduction: is the red dwarf listed here as G 158−27, also known as LHS 2. It is a slowly rotating, relatively inactive star in Cetus.

sections.title: Two Earth-mass neighbors
sections.text: Two planets announced in 2022 have minimum masses close to Earth’s and orbit within the star’s habitable zone. They were detected through radial velocities rather than transits, so their radii and surface conditions are not measured.

sections.title: A useful nearby target
sections.text: The combination of proximity and low activity makes the system attractive for future attempts to separate planetary light from starlight. “Habitable zone” describes the available stellar heating, not a detection of water or life.

10pc-0098.name: DENIS 0255−4700
10pc-0098.introduction: is a very faint late-L brown dwarf in Eridanus, near the transition to the cooler T spectral class. It was identified through the DENIS infrared survey.

sections.title: An exceptionally rapid spin
sections.text: It rotates in about 1.7 hours, far faster than the Sun. Rapid rotation and its nearby location make it useful for studying how brown dwarf atmospheres and spectral features change across the visible hemisphere.

sections.title: Too faint for ordinary stargazing
sections.text: Its proximity was established by parallax measurements published in 2006. Almost all of its detectable energy is infrared; its mass estimate depends strongly on the uncertain age used in cooling models.

10pc-0099.name: Groombridge 1618
10pc-0099.introduction: is the orange dwarf cataloged here as HD 88230, in Ursa Major. Its late-K spectrum lies near the boundary between orange and red dwarfs.

sections.title: A near miss for naked-eye viewing
sections.text: At visual magnitude about 6.6 it sits near the limit of unaided vision under excellent dark skies. Its large apparent motion made it an early target for attempts to measure stellar parallax.

sections.title: Spots and flares
sections.text: Rotating starspots produce small brightness changes, and flares have also been recorded. It provides a nearby example of magnetic behavior in a star cooler and less luminous than the Sun.

gj-412.name: Gliese 412
gj-412.introduction: is a wide red-dwarf binary in Ursa Major. The catalog’s BD+44 2051 A is the brighter primary; WX Ursae Majoris is its much smaller B component.

sections.title: Very different magnetic personalities
sections.text: WX UMa is a flare star and a detected X-ray source. The brighter primary is less conspicuous at high energies, illustrating how differently two related red dwarfs can behave.

sections.title: A wide stellar partnership
sections.text: Their projected separation is roughly 150 astronomical units. This is a true common-motion pair; the large apparent brightness difference does not mean that the stars lie at very different distances.

10pc-0102.name: AD Leonis
10pc-0102.introduction: is an intensely active red dwarf in Leo, also called Gliese 388. It is a frequently studied example of a nearby flare star.

sections.title: A laboratory for stellar eruptions
sections.text: Its flares have been observed across the electromagnetic spectrum, including X-rays. Strong magnetic fields, extensive active regions and hot coronal loops make it valuable for investigating how eruptions affect a star’s surroundings.

sections.title: Rotation mistaken for a planet
sections.text: A roughly 2.2-day radial-velocity signal was once proposed as a planet. Later studies attributed it to stellar activity linked to the star’s rapid rotation, showing why a periodic wobble needs independent checks.

10pc-0103.name: GJ 832
10pc-0103.introduction: is a red dwarf in Grus with a giant planet on a wide orbit. Its slow stellar rotation contrasts with some of the rapidly spinning flare stars in the neighborhood.

sections.title: A long planetary year
sections.text: GJ 832 b takes about a decade to complete an orbit. It was found by following the star’s slow radial-velocity changes over many years, rather than by photographing a resolved planetary disk.

sections.title: A supposed super-Earth reexamined
sections.text: The closer planet GJ 832 c, announced in 2014, was later challenged. Reanalysis found its signal consistent with stellar activity, so the often-repeated picture of a confirmed habitable-zone super-Earth is unreliable.

keid.name: 40 Eridani
keid.introduction: is a triple system combining the orange dwarf Keid, the white dwarf B and the red dwarf C. The catalog’s DY Eridani is component C.

sections.title: Three stars, three different states
sections.text: B and C form a pair far from A. In 1910, B’s white spectrum despite its feeble brightness helped reveal the existence of white dwarfs: extremely compact stars with hot surfaces but little emitting area.

sections.title: The real star behind Vulcan
sections.text: Keid is associated with the fictional home of Spock in Star Trek. A real planet announced around A in 2018 attracted attention, but later studies traced the roughly 42-day signal to stellar activity rather than a confirmed “Vulcan.”

source.title: NASA: Spock’s home planet goes ‘poof’

10pc-0106.name: GJ 682
10pc-0106.introduction: is a nearby red dwarf in Scorpius, seen against a much more distant and crowded region of the Milky Way. Its apparent proximity to background objects is a line-of-sight effect.

sections.title: Planet claims under revision
sections.text: Two planets proposed in 2014 were not recovered by a 2020 reanalysis, which favored stellar activity as the source of the signals. A separate giant-companion hint reported in 2026 has very uncertain mass and orbit, and remains evidence to investigate rather than a well-characterized planet.

10pc-0112.name: EV Lacertae
10pc-0112.introduction: is a faint red dwarf in Lacerta with an exceptionally energetic magnetic atmosphere. It is also known as Gliese 873.

sections.title: A flare that triggered Swift
sections.text: On April 25, 2008, NASA’s Swift satellite detected an eruption thousands of times stronger than the largest observed solar flares. A star normally too faint for unaided viewing briefly became an extraordinary high-energy source.

source.title: NASA: Pipsqueak star unleashes monster flare

sections.title: Small star, strong magnetic field
sections.text: Rapid rotation and a churning interior sustain a powerful magnetic field. EV Lac is a reminder that a low steady luminosity says little about how violent an individual stellar eruption can be.

ei-cancri.name: EI Cancri
ei-cancri.introduction: is a binary of two very low-mass red dwarfs in Cancer, also known as GJ 1116. Both are cool, faint stars near the lower end of the main sequence.

sections.title: Two ultracool siblings
sections.text: The components have late-M spectra and orbit at a separation of several astronomical units. Studying both together helps test models of stars close to the minimum mass for sustained hydrogen burning.

sections.title: An incompletely explored family
sections.text: A search for a third star published in 2015 was inconclusive. The established description is a binary; an additional component should not be counted as confirmed.

msc-18055+0230.name: 70 Ophiuchi
msc-18055+0230.introduction: is a nearby pair of orange dwarfs in Ophiuchus. A small telescope can separate the two stars, which orbit one another in roughly 88 years.

sections.title: An early test of stellar gravity
sections.text: William Herschel studied it as a physical double star. Its orbital motion helped demonstrate that the same gravitational laws used in the Solar System also apply to stars.

sections.title: An early planet claim
sections.text: In 1855, William Stephen Jacob proposed a planetary companion to explain apparent irregularities in the binary’s orbit. The claim did not hold up, but it marks an early attempt to find exoplanets through astrometry.

10pc-0117.name: Altair
10pc-0117.introduction: is the bright, nearby A-type star in Aquila and one corner of the Summer Triangle. Its rapid rotation makes it markedly different from a spherical, uniformly bright star.

sections.title: Flattened by rotation
sections.text: Altair spins in less than a day. Its equator bulges outward and is cooler and dimmer than its poles, an effect called gravity darkening. Interferometers have resolved this uneven surface directly.

sections.title: The cowherd star
sections.text: In Chinese tradition Altair represents the Cowherd, separated from the Weaver Girl, Vega, by the Milky Way. The related Japanese story is celebrated at Tanabata. Its Arabic-derived name refers to a flying eagle.

10pc-0118.name: WISE 1506+7027
10pc-0118.introduction: is the T6 brown dwarf cataloged here as 2MASS J15065257+7027247. It lies in Ursa Minor and emits most strongly in infrared light.

sections.title: Two survey names, one moving object
sections.text: It was recognized in WISE data in 2011. Its large proper motion explains why coordinates encoded in names from different observing epochs are noticeably different; they do not identify separate objects.

sections.title: A nearby cool atmosphere
sections.text: Its temperature is roughly 1,000 K, much cooler than a red dwarf’s photosphere. Methane absorption shapes its T-type spectrum, allowing comparisons with other nearby brown dwarfs at similar temperatures.

10pc-0119.name: G 99−49
10pc-0119.introduction: is a magnetically active red dwarf in Orion, also called GJ 3379. It is a foreground neighbor, unrelated to the distant massive stars that dominate Orion’s familiar shape.

sections.title: Once closer than Alpha Centauri is now
sections.text: Calculations of its motion indicate that it passed roughly four light-years from the Sun about 160,000 years ago. Today it is much farther away and moving outward.

sections.title: A fast-spinning red dwarf
sections.text: It rotates in about 1.8 days and has a strong measured magnetic field. Small changes as surface features rotate into view reveal activity on a star far too distant to resolve as a conventional surface image.

10pc-0120.name: DENIS J0817−6155
10pc-0120.introduction: is the T6 brown dwarf listed here as 2MASS J08173001−6155158. It is a nearby infrared source in Carina.

sections.title: Hidden near the Galactic plane
sections.text: A comparison of DENIS and 2MASS survey data revealed this overlooked brown dwarf in 2010. It is relatively bright in near-infrared light but had escaped earlier searches in a crowded part of the sky.

sections.title: A useful atmospheric target
sections.text: Its accessible infrared brightness makes detailed spectroscopy possible. The spectrum probes molecular absorption in a cool atmosphere, providing a comparison for fainter brown dwarfs that are much harder to observe.

10pc-0121.name: Gliese 445
10pc-0121.introduction: is the red dwarf listed here as G 254−29, in Camelopardalis. Its substantial motion toward the Solar System will change its place in the nearby-star rankings.

sections.title: A distant future encounter with Voyager
sections.text: In about 40,000 years, Voyager 1 is expected to pass within roughly 1.6 light-years of Gliese 445. That is a wide interstellar flyby, not a planned rendezvous or an entry into a planetary system.

sections.title: The neighborhood changes
sections.text: By then the star itself will be much closer to the Sun than it is today. Nearby-star lists are snapshots: stellar motion continually brings new objects closer while carrying others away.

10pc-0122.name: WISEA J1540−5101
10pc-0122.introduction: is a nearby late-M red dwarf in the southern constellation Norma, listed here as WISEA J154045.67−510139.3.

source.title: Kirkpatrick et al. 2016: The AllWISE Motion Survey, Part 2

sections.title: A star found by its motion
sections.text: The AllWISE Motion Survey identified this previously overlooked neighbor in 2014. Follow-up spectra showed a cool M-type star, and later observations refined the optical classification to M6.5.

sections.title: WISE did not find only brown dwarfs
sections.text: Despite its WISE name, this object is a red dwarf rather than a T- or Y-type brown dwarf. Its discovery showed that even comparatively bright nearby infrared sources could still escape recognition in earlier surveys.

10pc-0123.name: 2MASS 0939−2448
10pc-0123.introduction: is a very cold T-type brown dwarf source in Antlia. Its full designation is 2MASS J09393548−2448279, and its multiplicity remains an important uncertainty.

sections.title: Possibly two objects in one point of light
sections.text: A 2008 analysis found that its luminosity and atmospheric temperature were difficult to reconcile as one brown dwarf. An unresolved pair of cooler, lower-luminosity objects could explain the mismatch.

source.title: Burgasser et al. 2008: A possible cold brown dwarf binary

sections.title: Why the distinction matters
sections.text: Splitting the observed light between two components changes the inferred radii and masses. The proposed binary explanation is not a resolved measurement of two individual objects, so component properties remain model-dependent.

10pc-0124.name: GJ 3323
10pc-0124.introduction: is a red dwarf in Eridanus, also called LHS 1723. Emission lines and X-rays reveal magnetic activity in this otherwise inconspicuous nearby star.

sections.title: Two reported planetary signals
sections.text: A 2017 HARPS analysis reported a close-in small planet, b, and a longer-period candidate, c. The inner planet has a year of only about five days; the outer signal is less securely established.

sections.title: A fully convective interior
sections.text: At its low mass, heat is transported by convection throughout the interior rather than in a Sun-like outer layer alone. Such stars are useful for studying how magnetic fields work in a different internal structure.

10pc-0127.name: HD 119850
10pc-0127.introduction: is a red dwarf in Boötes, better known in nearby-star research as Gliese 526. It is also cataloged as Wolf 498.

sections.title: A relatively bright red-dwarf target
sections.text: Its early-M spectrum and proximity make it accessible for detailed study compared with the much fainter late-M stars in this catalog. Even so, it radiates only a few percent of the Sun’s total energy.

sections.title: Looking for leftover dust
sections.text: Infrared observations have searched for extra emission from a surrounding debris disk without establishing such an excess. A nondetection limits warm dust visible to that survey; it does not show that the star has no smaller orbiting bodies.

stein-2051.name: Stein 2051
stein-2051.introduction: is a wide binary in Camelopardalis containing a red dwarf, A, and a white dwarf, B. The white dwarf is fainter in visible light despite being more massive.

sections.title: A natural gravitational scale
sections.text: Hubble followed the apparent deflection of a distant background star as Stein 2051 B passed close to its line of sight in 2014. The analysis, published in 2017, measured B at about 0.675 solar masses.

source.title: Sahu et al. 2017: Relativistic deflection measures a white dwarf’s mass

sections.title: A puzzle resolved
sections.text: Earlier, uncertain orbital estimates had raised the possibility of an unusual iron-core white dwarf. The microlensing mass instead agreed with the ordinary carbon–oxygen-core interpretation and the expected white dwarf mass–radius relation.

10pc-0130.name: 2MASS 1114−2618
10pc-0130.introduction: is a late-T brown dwarf in Hydra, listed here as 2MASS J11145133−2618235. It was identified in the 2MASS search for methane-bearing brown dwarfs.

sections.title: A cool, chemically revealing spectrum
sections.text: Its T7.5 spectrum contains strong molecular absorption. Atmospheric studies have found it relatively poor in heavy elements, with inferred temperature and gravity depending on the models used.

sections.title: A fast-moving infrared neighbor
sections.text: Its position changes by roughly three arcseconds a year against distant background sources. Matching its motion across surveys helps establish that detections at different positions belong to the same nearby object.

10pc-0131.name: Wolf 294
10pc-0131.introduction: is the nearby red dwarf also known as Gliese 251, in Gemini. It is a frequent target of precision radial-velocity surveys.

sections.title: A planetary picture that changed
sections.text: A 2020 analysis rejected two earlier proposed signals and established the approximately 14-day super-Earth GJ 251 b. A second candidate super-Earth, c, was reported in 2025 on a roughly 54-day orbit in the star’s habitable zone.

source.title: Beard et al. 2025: A nearby habitable-zone super-Earth candidate

sections.title: A target for future telescopes
sections.text: The combination of proximity and a temperate-orbit candidate makes the system interesting for future direct-imaging instruments. No surface water or life has been detected, and radial-velocity measurements alone do not determine the proposed worlds’ radii.

10pc-0133.name: LP 816−60
10pc-0133.introduction: is a nearby M-type red dwarf in Capricornus. Its name comes from the Luyten–Palomar proper-motion surveys.

sections.title: A long magnetic cycle
sections.text: Observations indicate a starspot cycle of roughly 11 years, similar in duration to the Sun’s familiar activity cycle. Following such slow changes helps distinguish stellar magnetic variability from long-period companion signals.

sections.title: A neighbor with a survey name
sections.text: It was included in Luyten’s 1979 NLTT catalog of moving stars. Its understated designation reflects how many nearby red dwarfs became known through systematic surveys rather than naked-eye sky traditions.

10pc-0134.name: WISE 0350−5658
10pc-0134.introduction: is a very cold Y1 brown dwarf in Reticulum, listed here as WISE J035000.32−565830.2. It was discovered in WISE data in 2012.

sections.title: Closer to planetary temperatures
sections.text: Atmosphere studies place its effective temperature around 325–350 K. Such temperatures are far below stellar photospheres; the object is observed mainly through infrared light rather than a visible stellar glow.

sections.title: Chemistry out of equilibrium
sections.text: Models including atmospheric mixing reproduce its spectrum better than models in complete chemical equilibrium. Its uncertain age leaves a broad mass range, potentially overlapping the masses of giant planets.

10pc-0135.name: LSR J1835+3259
10pc-0135.introduction: is the ultracool dwarf listed here as 2MASSI J1835379+325954, in Lyra. It lies near the boundary between very low-mass stars and massive brown dwarfs.

sections.title: Auroras beyond the Solar System
sections.text: Radio and optical observations reported in 2015 revealed auroral activity. Charged particles interacting with its atmosphere produce a phenomenon more reminiscent of Jupiter’s auroras than ordinary stellar flares.

sections.title: A resolved radiation belt
sections.text: In 2023, a worldwide radio array imaged a double-lobed radiation belt around it. This showed high-energy particles trapped in its magnetic environment, analogous to Jupiter’s belts but much more luminous.

source.title: UC Santa Cruz: First radiation belt observed outside the Solar System

10pc-0136.name: HD 36395
10pc-0136.introduction: is a nearby red dwarf in Orion, also called Gliese 205. It lies in the foreground of the much more distant stars and clouds associated with the constellation.

sections.title: A detailed magnetic target
sections.text: Its relative brightness makes it useful for studying red-dwarf magnetic fields and rotation. A rotation period of roughly 34 days has been measured through changes associated with stellar activity.

sections.title: Planet candidates reexamined
sections.text: Two radial-velocity candidates were proposed in a 2019 preprint. A 2023 study found no convincing planetary evidence, emphasizing the need to model the star’s own changing spectrum before interpreting small signals as companions.

10pc-0137.name: 2MASS 0415−0935
10pc-0137.introduction: is a cold T8 brown dwarf in Eridanus. The catalog uses the older 2MASSI J0415195−093506 designation for the same object.

sections.title: A spectral yardstick
sections.text: It was among the discoveries used in 2002 to extend the T-dwarf sequence to subtype T8. It has since served as an important comparison object for studies of still colder brown dwarfs.

sections.title: Molecules instead of a solar spectrum
sections.text: Methane and water absorption dominate much of its infrared spectrum. Atmospheric analyses also investigate ammonia and departures from chemical equilibrium, connecting the physics of cool brown dwarfs with giant-planet atmospheres.

gj-229.name: Gliese 229
gj-229.introduction: is a red dwarf with a remarkable brown-dwarf companion system in Lepus. The object historically called Gliese 229 B is actually the close pair Ba and Bb.

sections.title: A landmark methane discovery
sections.text: In 1995, methane in the companion’s spectrum supplied clear evidence for a cool substellar object, helping establish brown dwarfs as a real population between stars and giant planets.

sections.title: The famous companion was twins
sections.text: Observations reported in 2024 resolved the long-standing puzzle of B’s unusually low brightness for its mass: Ba and Bb orbit each other about every 12 days. Their combined light had been mistaken for one object for nearly three decades.

source.title: Caltech: It’s twins! Mystery of famed brown dwarf solved
